extracted.intended_audience: physicians, neurologists, medical students, and artists studying nerve-muscular expression and clinical observation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for observing, describing, and interpreting muscular movements, postures, and facial/ocular signs as indices of brain and nerve‑center states in patients (including infants and the chronically ill). Intended to inform clinical localization and descriptive practice for physicians and artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression effected by muscular action
rubrics_metrics.description: All expression of feeling is effected by muscular action, whether it be by words, by facial movement or gesture, movements effected by voluntary muscles; or expression may be produced by dilatation of the pupil, erection of the hair, or disturbed action of the heart, these being due to the conditions of inorganic muscular fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish voluntary muscular expressions (face, gesture, speech) from involuntary/autonomic changes (pupil, hair erection, cardiac changes) when interpreting the state of the nervous system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movements depend on nerve‑muscular stimuli from nerve‑centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements depend upon nerve‑muscular stimuli originating in nerve‑centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the principle that observable movements reflect underlying nerve‑center activity when seeking signs by which to describe 'nervous cases.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscular conditions as indicators of nervous system state
rubrics_metrics.description: We commonly judge of the state of the nervous system by muscular conditions (examples: stooping attitude and spiritless gait of a tired man vs same individual when rested; incipient intoxication indicated by reeling gait, unsteady hand, and muscular tremor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a patient's current posture/movements to their normal/rested state; specific changes (gait, tremor, posture) suggest particular functional states such as fatigue or intoxication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head position and asymmetrical gesture as signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Position of the head indicates expression — firmly upright in defiance, drooping in shame; commonly held on one side in nervous women and girls convalescent from chorea, an example of an asymmetrical gesture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note head carriage and asymmetry as potential markers of nervous disorders (e.g., chorea) or emotional states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training of skilled hand/face indicates brain condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist's brush, sculptor's modeling-tool, pianist's and violinist's finger-touch indicate the training and actual condition of the working of his brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine motor skill and refinement of movement reflect cerebral development/training; include occupational context when interpreting hand movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant nerve‑muscular phenomena record nervous system condition
rubrics_metrics.description: In the infant the condition of the nervous system is best recorded in terms of nerve‑muscular phenomena (laughing, playfulness, reflex actions, eye movements when looking at an object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In infants prioritize observation of reflexes, eye tracking, sucking, and spontaneous movements to assess cerebral adequacy and potential pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal eye movements and associated brain‑centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal eye movements — pupil response to light, accommodation for near/distant vision, turning of the eyes while maintaining parallelism — are supposed to be governed by particular brain‑centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test pupil reactivity, accommodation, and coordinated eye movement; loss or distortion implicates specific brain centers or depressed consciousness (e.g., chloroform anaesthesia, coma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of associated eye movements as pathological sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated movements of the eyes may be completely lost in deep anaesthesia, in coma from alcoholism, or in profound infant sleep; loss may be detected in weakly infants while awake, in meningitis and other coarse brain‑disease, and sometimes chronic in paralyzed/idiotic persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect absence or asymmetry of coordinated ocular movement as a sign of cerebral dysfunction; note reversibility with returning consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic features of nystagmus
rubrics_metrics.description: In nystagmus the eyeballs oscillate rapidly (usually horizontal, rarely vertical); the parallelism of the axes is generally maintained; specific directional deficits may coexist with preserved convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe direction of oscillation, preservation of parallelism, and convergence behaviour to infer localization or specific brain‑center damage (per Ferrier's theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizontal vs vertical eye movements and 'intellectuality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Most ordinary eye movements are probably horizontal and least voluntary/simple; vertical movements are more complex, calling special muscles into play, and may therefore be considered more intellectual. Moving the eyes in their orbits is more intellectual than turning the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether patients move eyes within the orbits or move the head to direct gaze; the former suggests higher ocular motor control and alertness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial movements symmetry and zones of intellectual expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements of the face are generally symmetrical; asymmetry is seen in facial palsy, sneering, and one‑sided grimaces. Intellectuality appears most commonly expressed in the frontal and middle zones and by the corrugator and orbicularis oculi muscles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess symmetry and action of specific facial muscle groups (frontal/mid-face) as indicators of mental state or localized facial nerve dysfunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial muscle tonus and expression as signs of suffering or distress
rubrics_metrics.description: Facial appearance can be a physical sign of mental as well as physical and organic suffering; in headache the orbicular muscle and adjacent parts are flabby, skin hanging loosely; laughter restores tone and removes expression of headache temporarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe eyelid tonus, skin laxity around eyes, and changes with affect (e.g., laughter) to infer transient vs persistent distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life of the eyes given by eyelids and periorbital muscles
rubrics_metrics.description: The life of the eyes is given, not by the eyeball, but by conditions of the eyelids and of the muscles that move them, and in some degree by the muscles which move the eyeballs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on eyelid tone, blink, and periocular muscle function when judging 'expressiveness' and underlying neural control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free/disengaged hand as expressive vs engaged hand
rubrics_metrics.description: When the hand is left free and disengaged (as the hand of the orator) it unconsciously expresses by its position or movement the general mental state; a hand engaged in holding an object or manipulation is directed to accomplish the aim and is not simply indicative of the condition of the brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer observation of free hand posture and gesture for clues to mental state; treat hands engaged in tasks as less diagnostic for mood/mental condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nervous hand posture (characteristic description)
rubrics_metrics.description: A very nervous child or one convalescent from chorea holds out its hands in front level with the shoulder with fingers spread; palms turned down, wrist droops slightly; metacarpo‑phalangeal joints moderately extended, first and second internodes flexed or straight, thumb extended backward and somewhat abducted; frequent finger twitching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this constellation of finger and wrist positions as a recognizable sign of nervousness or choreic convalescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energetic/powerful hand and ortho‑extension as sign of strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The ortho‑extended hand (axes of metacarpal bones and digits in same plane with forearm) is the energetic position, seen in healthy children running to meet a friend; energetic hand characteristic of healthful nerve‑muscular condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify ortho‑extension as an index of vigor/mental energy; contrast with closed convulsive hand (thumb turned in) which indicates predisposition to convulsions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finger twitching varieties as diagnostic signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties of finger‑twitching: (1) Flexor‑extensor — primary flexion then extension (e.g., 'picking the bedclothes' in typhoid preceding coma); (2) Extensor‑flexor — primary extension then flexion (common in slight chorea and nervous children; subsultus tendinum in typhoid); (3) Abductor‑adductor — lateral separation of fingers then drawn together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify observed finger movements into these types to help identify underlying conditions (typhoid exhaustion, chorea, nervous states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Head movement classification and clinical significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements of the head classified as flexion/extension, rotation (head erect), and inclination (depression of one side). Inclination sometimes indicates weakness and is frequently seen in young girls and weakly persons; specific inclination patterns are common in choreic girls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe head carriage, ability to hold head erect (especially in infants), and patterns of inclination/rotation for clues to weakness, chorea, or cerebral adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cranial nerve‑related muscular signs (teeth, tongue, jaw, vagus effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tooth‑grinding, champing of the jaws, and trismus are signs of disordered conditions of the fifth nerve. Violent motions of the tongue in chorea and whooping‑cough, tremulous tongue of alcoholism and paralyses indicate affections of the seventh nerve. Affections of the pneumogastric may produce palpitations, irregularities of organic action, bronchial spasm of asthma, and functional aphasia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map specific orofacial and visceral manifestations to likely cranial nerve involvement (V, VII, X) when localizing pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torso posture, gait and lower extremity signs for spinal/localization
rubrics_metrics.description: Children and adult patients often 'hold themselves awkwardly' — stoop or give the spine an ill‑balanced position due to want of nerve‑muscular energy characteristic of exhaustion and weakness. Gait and manner in walking may be characteristic of brain or cord disease; conditions affecting muscles of both lower extremities are usually dependent upon disease of the cord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use torso posture and detailed gait analysis to distinguish cerebral vs spinal disease; examine leg muscles and reflexes to localize spinal lesions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reflex actions as localization indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflex actions are used as a means of localizing and ascertaining the condition of the nerve‑centers; visible muscular conditions are the indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate reflex testing with observation of visible muscular signs to improve localization of lesions in the nervous system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for observation and description
rubrics_metrics.description: When we see in the face, limbs, or body indications of his brain or mental condition, we should analyze and describe — first, the position of features and parts as we see them, then the muscles which produce those positions or movements, knowing that the muscular condition which has produced the movements or positions is the result of the state of the corresponding nerve‑centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a two‑step descriptive approach: (1) record visible positions/movements precisely, (2) identify the muscles producing them, and (3) infer nerve‑center involvement. Compare with post‑mortem lesions and collect many cases to strengthen clinicopathologic correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary observation: artist and physician collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a field for observation and description in which the artist and the physician may work together, observing and analyzing with as much exactness as may be the mode by which varying conditions of the brain and mind are indicated to our eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage collaboration with artists (drawing, sculpture) to improve accuracy and nuance in recording muscular expressions for clinical and descriptive purposes.
